g.text: The ordering gate has to live INSIDE the claim statement - not as a check before it
'Read whether the prior sequence is terminal, then claim if so' is two steps that look harmless in isolation and reopen the exact race the gate exists to close.
Retries are a SELF-LOOP, not a distinct state - and that is what keeps the claim query to one predicate
pending
succeeded
dead_lettered
a failed attempt keeps the row in pending
with an updated next_attempt_at
WHERE status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= NOW()
ONE predicate, whether this is a delivery's first attempt or its ninth. A distinct
'retrying' state would mean the claim query had to enumerate which states are
claimable - and every new state would be a new place to forget one.
SubscriptionRepository -> SqlSubscriptionRepository
findActiveForEventType(eventType, tenantId) # the fan-out match
getById(subscriptionId) # read FRESH at every attempt, never cached
DeliveryRepository -> SqlDeliveryRepository
insertFanOut(eventId, subscriptionId, sequenceNumber) # idempotent
claimNextDue(workerId, limit) # bounded and SEQUENCE-GATED
recordAttempt(deliveryId, outcome, nextAttemptAt | terminal)
HttpDeliveryClient -> DefaultHttpDeliveryClient
send(url, signedPayload, headers, timeout) # NEVER follows redirects
Signer -> HmacSha256Signer sign(secret, timestamp, payload)
CircuitBreakerRegistry -> PerSubscriptionCircuitBreaker
isOpen / recordSuccess / recordFailure # PER SUBSCRIPTION, never global
RetryPolicy -> ExponentialBackoffWithJitter nextAttemptAt(attemptNumber)
DeliveryWorker is the orchestrator: it depends on all six interfaces and implements
none of the storage, network or coordination itself.
Two details in that list are decisions rather than plumbing. getById is read FRESH
at every attempt and never cached across retries - a customer who rotates their
signing secret or changes their endpoint mid-retry-schedule should have the next
attempt honour it. And the breaker is keyed PER SUBSCRIPTION: one subscriber's
dead endpoint must never open a breaker that stops delivery to anyone else.
The claim query, as ONE atomic statement
UPDATE deliveries SET claimed_by = :worker_id
WHERE status = 'pending'
AND next_attempt_at <= NOW()
AND NOT EXISTS ( -- THE ORDERING GATE
SELECT 1 FROM deliveries prior
WHERE prior.subscription_id = deliveries.subscription_id
AND prior.sequence_number = deliveries.sequence_number - 1
AND prior.status = 'pending' -- prior is not terminal yet
ORDER BY next_attempt_at
LIMIT :limit
RETURNING *
The NOT EXISTS clause is the ENTIRE ordering guarantee, and it is worth being
precise about why it has to live inside the claim rather than in front of it: a
separate 'is the prior sequence terminal?' read followed by a separate claim is
exactly the check-then-act race - the prior row could still be MID-COMMIT between
the two steps.
Folding the gate into the same WHERE clause the claim itself uses makes 'is N+1
eligible' and 'claim N+1' ONE ATOMIC DECISION.
And note what counts as terminal: succeeded OR dead_lettered. Giving up on
sequence N is what unblocks N+1 - so a permanently broken delivery delays the
queue by its retry schedule, not forever.
for delivery in due:
subscription = subscriptionRepo.getById(delivery.subscription_id)
if circuitBreaker.isOpen(subscription.id):
recordAttempt(delivery.id, 'skipped',
nextAttemptAt=retryPolicy.nextAttemptAt(attempts))
continue # fail fast - NO SOCKET against a known-dead endpoint
signature = signer.sign(subscription.secret, timestamp, payload)
result = httpClient.send(subscription.endpoint_url, payload,
headers={'Webhook-Signature': f't={timestamp},v1={signature}',
'Webhook-Id': delivery.id},
timeout=SUBSCRIBER_TIMEOUT)
if result.ok:
recordAttempt(delivery.id, 'succeeded') # terminal: unblocks N+1
elif delivery.attempt_count >= MAX_ATTEMPTS:
recordAttempt(delivery.id, 'dead_lettered') # terminal: unblocks N+1
else:
recordAttempt(delivery.id, 'retry_scheduled',
nextAttemptAt=retryPolicy.nextAttemptAt(attempts))
claimNextDue needs no application-level lock, for the same reason the job scheduler
and payments both push their claims down to the database: many worker instances
run concurrently, and a language-level mutex only protects threads on the SAME
instance - it does nothing about a different instance claiming the same row a
moment later. Correctness comes entirely from the conditional UPDATE's WHERE
clause, evaluated by the database as one statement.
Webhook-Id is what makes at-least-once delivery safe for the subscriber: it is the
idempotency key they deduplicate on. And Webhook-Signature carries the timestamp
INSIDE the signed material, so a captured payload cannot be replayed later against
the same signature.
Four error cases designed for deliberately
the subscriber processed the request, but the response never came back
a dropped connection, or a read timeout after they had already returned 200 - genuinely ambiguous from this side, and unlike
a payments processor there is NO STATUS API to query for the true outcome: the subscriber's server IS the ground truth, and
it is not queryable after the fact. So the deliberate choice is to retry anyway and rely on their idempotent handling of
Webhook-Id - favouring at-least-once over risking at-most-once, because a silently dropped event is worse than a harmless
duplicate.
the endpoint returns a 3xx redirect
NEVER follow it. Treat it as a failure and retry against the original URL. Following a redirect would forward the signed
payload - and implicitly, evidence of the signing secret's effect - to a host the subscriber never explicitly registered: a
real SSRF-adjacent risk this design closes by refusing the hop entirely.
a subscription's filter no longer matches by the time a worker attempts it
the customer changed their subscribed event types after this event was ingested. The delivery row is HONOURED AS A COMMITMENT
ALREADY MADE at fan-out time, not retroactively cancelled - the config that mattered was the config at ingestion, and
re-checking it at delivery time would make 'did this get sent' depend on exactly when a worker got to it.
the endpoint is slow but eventually returns 2xx, right against the timeout
SUBSCRIBER_TIMEOUT has to sit well below the smallest gap in the retry schedule - the one-second first-retry gap - or a
handful of slow-but-alive endpoints tie up worker capacity for longer than an entire early retry cycle is meant to take.
Patterns, named
Repository DeliveryRepository and SubscriptionRepository hide storage behind method calls; DeliveryWorker never
issues SQL directly
Strategy RetryPolicy, Signer and HttpDeliveryClient are each swappable behind one interface without the worker
knowing or caring which concrete implementation is wired in
State, via an enum pending -> succeeded | dead_lettered, with retries as a SELF-LOOP rather than a separate state
Circuit breaker keyed PER SUBSCRIPTION rather than globally - isolating one dependency's failure from every other
Idempotent consumer the fan-out writer's unique constraint on (event_id, subscription_id) is this pattern applied to the
ingestion side: a redelivered bus message produces the SAME fan-out rows, not duplicates -
complementing, rather than re-deriving, the transactional outbox the producing service used to get
the event onto the bus in the first place
